name: The Tree of Life (Kabbalah)
desc: Ten luminous sefirot linked by twenty-two paths, traced to the Zohar and the medieval book Bahir — the canonical diagram of the Kabbalistic Tree of Life.
credit: Diagram after the Bahir / Zohar; public domain

name: Kircher's Tree of Life
desc: Athanasius Kircher's engraved Tree of Life from Oedipus Aegyptiacus, fusing the ten sefirot with the Tree of Jesse and Egyptian cosmology into a single allegorical system.
credit: Engraving by Athanasius Kircher, S.J.; public domain

name: Tree of Jesse (Chartres Rose)
desc: The Tree of Jesse from the west-rose window of Chartres Cathedral: Christ at the crown, the patriarchs in the branches, and the kings of Judah in the roots — a stained-glass genealogy of salvation.
credit: Chartres Cathedral glass; public domain (photo C. H. Moore, 1840–1930)

name: Bernward Doors — Christ on the Tree of Life
desc: The Bernward Doors, bronze gate of Hildesheim Cathedral: Christ on the Tree of Life, flanked by the Fall in Eden and the Redemption in Gethsemane — an Ottonian statement of the cross as the tree of life.
credit: Bronze by the workshop of Bernward of Hildesheim; photo © Bishop's Press Office Hildesheim, CC BY

name: Chi-Rho Page, Book of Kells
desc: The Chi-Rho page of the Book of Kells, the IHS monogram of the Word wrapped in interlaced vines, knots and tendrils — an Insular gospel book where the living tree becomes woven ornament.
credit: Book of Kells, Irish scribes; public domain

name: Adam and Eve under the Tree of Life (Doré)
desc: Gustave Doré's 'Adam and Eve under the Tree of Life': the serpent on the forbidden tree and the Tree of Life beyond, an engraved illustration from his edition of the Bible.
credit: Wood engraving by Gustave Doré; public domain

name: Ishtar Gate & Processional Way
desc: The glazed-brick lion procession of the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, where sacred trees and lions line the processional way — the garden of Marduk rendered in blue brick.
credit: Ishtar Gate, Nebuchadnezzar II; photo © 0x010C, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Stele of the Vultures
desc: The Stele of the Vultures: Gudea of Lagash laying out his temple, with a sacred tree and the vultures of the underworld — Sumerian royal iconography of the sacred tree.
credit: Stele of Gudea, Louvre; photo © Kikuyu3, CC BY-SA 4.0
artist:
Background: Kikuyu3
Elements: Eric Gaba (User:Sting)

Composite: पाटलिपुत्र (talk) 10:52, 30 April 2020 (UTC)

name: Thutmose III and the Tree of Heaven
location: Tomb of Thutmose III, Valley of the Kings
desc: Thutmose III seated beneath the sycamore (the 'tree of heaven') of Hathor, the goddess of the West — the Egyptian sacred tree of the afterlife in a Theban tomb painting.
credit: Wall painting, Valley of the Kings; public domain

name: Buddha beneath the Bodhi Tree
desc: The Buddha beneath the Bodhi tree at Jamal Garhi: the wheel of dharma turning, the tree of awakening that frames the first sermon — Greco-Buddhist schist sculpture of the Enlightenment.
credit: Gandharan schist, 2nd c. CE; photo © SpeakingArch, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Penglai, the Island of the Immortals
desc: Penglai, the island of the Immortals rising from the sea, with the peach tree of immortality — a Tang-dynasty tradition of the celestial tree of eternal life in the far-east seas.
credit: After Li Sixun (Li Po-chun); public domain

name: Bronze Money Tree (Sanxingdui)
desc: A bronze Money Tree from the Sanxingdui culture: a three-branched trunk crowned with perched birds, a dragon and jade — a Han-world axis mundi of wealth and the cosmos.
credit: Bronze, Sanxingdui Museum; photo © Gary Todd, CC0

name: The Ceiba of Tikal (Axis Mundi)
desc: The great ceiba of Tikal, the Maya world-tree whose roots drink from Xibalba and whose canopy holds the gods — the living ceiba that the Classic Maya cities grew around.
credit: Ceiba pentandra, Tikal National Park; photo CC0 (Flickr)

name: Ghashghai Carpet — Tree of Life Medallion
desc: A 19th-century Shiraz (Ghashghai) carpet whose central medallion blooms with the Tree of Life, its branches unfurling pomegranates, roses and vine-scroll — the Persian carpet's garden of paradise.
credit: Shiraz weavers, 19th c.; photo CC0 (Hiart)

name: Kermanshah Carpet — Tree of Life
desc: A late-19th-century Kermanshah carpet: a serpentine Tree of Life flanked by the four paradises, its boughs heavy with fruit — the Persian garden-of-Paradise rendered in wool and silk.
credit: Kermanshah weavers, 19th c.; public domain

name: Tāne Mahuta, the Great Kauri
desc: Tāne Mahuta, the great kauri of the Waipoua Forest, the 'Guardian of the Forest' — one of the largest and oldest living trees on Earth, a Māori taonga (treasure) of the world-tree.
credit: Kauri (Agathis australis), Waipoua Forest; photo CC BY 2.0 (Flickr)

name: Yggdrasil (Heine)
desc: F. W. Heine's 'Yggdrasil': the great ash of the Norse cosmos, its branches over the nine worlds, with the dragon NídhoŁgn gnawing the roots — a 19th-century romantic revival of the world-tree.
credit: Oil by Friedrich Wilhelm Heine; public domain

name: Yggdrasil (Mundane Tree, Bagge)
desc: Oluf Bagge's 'Mundane Tree' (Yggdrasil): the ash of the Norse world, the eagle on its crown and the serpent in its roots — a mid-19th-century depiction of the nine-world axis.
credit: Oil by Oluf Bagge; public domain

name: Face-Towers of the Bayon
desc: The face-towers of the Bayon at Angkor, whose serene stone faces look out over the world-tree of the Khmer cosmos — the temple-mountain of Avalokiteshvara as a cosmic tree.
credit: Bayon temple, Angkor; photo © Arabsalam, CC BY-SA 3.0

name: St Agatha & the Tree of Life (Monreale)
desc: Saint Agatha enthroned beneath a Tree of Life in the apse mosaic of the Cathedral of Monreale, the Norman-Byzantine gold ground of paradise.
credit: Apse mosaic, Monreale Cathedral; photo © José Luiz, CC BY-SA 4.0

name: St Lawrence & the Tree of Life (Monreale)
desc: Saint Lawrence and the Tree of Life in the Monreale apse mosaic, a golden garden of paradise set in the Norman-Byzantine gold ground.
credit: Apse mosaic, Monreale Cathedral; public domain

name: Sacred Tree & Winged Genii (Nimrud)
desc: The Assyrian sacred tree flanked by winged genii with pollen cones, from Ashurnasirpal II's Northwest Palace — the palm-like world-axis at the heart of Assyrian royal ideology.
credit: Alabaster relief, Nimrud; photo public domain / CC

name: Cylinder Seal with the Sacred Tree
desc: A Mesopotamian cylinder seal cut with the sacred tree between gods and beasts — the garden of the gods worn on the wrist, rolled into eternity across clay.
credit: Cylinder seal impression; photo public domain / CC

name: Warka Vase
desc: The Warka Vase of Uruk: registers of water, grain, sheep and worshippers rising to the goddess Inanna — the oldest carved narrative of the land's abundance climbing like a tree toward heaven.
credit: Uruk ritual vase, Iraq Museum; photo public domain / CC

name: Etana and the Eagle
desc: The shepherd-king Etana carried heavenward on the eagle's back to fetch the plant of birth — the Mesopotamian ascent myth, stamped in miniature on a cylinder seal.
credit: Cylinder seal impression; photo public domain / CC

name: The Tree Goddess (Tomb of Sennedjem)
desc: The goddess Nut pouring water from the sycamore in the tomb of Sennedjem — the tree-goddess who quenches the souls of the dead at the edge of the western desert.
credit: Wall painting, Deir el-Medina; photo public domain / CC

name: Osiris Bed
desc: The Osiris bed: a wooden frame sown with grain that sprouts in the dark in the shape of the risen god — the Egyptian tree of death-and-return, greenness itself resurrected.
credit: Funerary object; photo public domain / CC

name: Menorah of Titus' Arch
desc: The seven-branched menorah carved on the Arch of Titus, carried from the burning Temple of Jerusalem — the menorah as the Tree of Life in exile, its branches remembered in stone.
credit: Marble relief, Rome; photo public domain / CC

name: Tree of Life — San Clemente Apse
desc: The apse mosaic of San Clemente in Rome: the crucified Christ rises as a vast acanthus Tree of Life, its coils filling heaven with deer, peacocks, shepherds and saints.
credit: Apse mosaic, Basilica San Clemente; photo public domain / CC

name: The Tree of Life — Otranto Floor
desc: The vast 12th-century mosaic floor of Otranto Cathedral: the Tree of Life running the whole nave's length, threaded with Alexander, Arthur, Adam and the beasts of every age.
credit: Mosaic floor, Otranto Cathedral; photo public domain / CC

name: Tree of Jesse Window (Saint-Denis)
desc: The Tree of Jesse window of Suger's Saint-Denis — the ancestor-tree of Christ bursting into glass and light, the origin of Gothic stained glass itself.
credit: Stained glass, Saint-Denis; photo public domain / CC

name: The Green Man
desc: The Green Man — the foliate face whose mouth pours vines, carved in a thousand churches — the old arboreal spirit folded into the margins of Christian stone.
credit: Medieval carving; photo public domain / CC

name: Mshatta Facade
location: Qasr al-Mshatta, Jordan (now Pergamon Museum, Berlin)
desc: The Mshatta facade: a mile of carved vines on the desert palace wall — the endless tree of life of Umayyad stonemasons, animals dissolving into its scroll.
credit: Carved facade, Pergamon Museum; photo public domain / CC

name: Tree of Life Tilework
desc: Safavid tilework trees — cypresses bending with birds in lapis and turquoise — the Persian garden of paradise fired onto the walls of Isfahan.
credit: Ceramic tile, Iran; photo public domain / CC

name: Tree of Life Silk (Safavid)
desc: A Safavid silk woven with the Tree of Life — hunters, simurghs and blossoming branches — paradise textile carried along the silk roads as diplomatic gold.
credit: Woven silk, Safavid; photo public domain / CC

name: Ottoman Tree of Life Textile
desc: Ottoman court weavers' Tree of Life — carnations, tulips and cypresses rising in silk and metal thread — the imperial garden of eternity.
credit: Woven textile, Ottoman; photo public domain / CC

name: Senmurv Silk
desc: The Sasanian silk with the senmurv — the dog-bird of the tree — circling the pearl-bordered Tree of Life, the royal emblem of a cosmic garden.
credit: Woven silk, Sasanian; photo public domain / CC

name: The Garden of Pasargadae
desc: Cyrus' garden at Pasargadae — the original chahar bagh, four rivers watering a planted paradise — the world's first designed garden as a tree of life in plan.
credit: Archaeological site, Iran; photo public domain / CC

name: The Enclosed Garden (Persian Miniature)
desc: A Timurid miniature of the enclosed garden — blossoming trees, watercourses and lovers — paradise painted as the Persians imagined the soul's destination.
credit: Manuscript painting; photo public domain / CC

name: Kalpavriksha — the Wishing Tree
desc: Kalpavriksha, the wish-fulfilling tree of Hindu and Jain cosmology — rooted in the churning of the milk ocean, granting every desire that reaches its shade.
credit: Indian painting; photo public domain / CC

name: The Great Banyan of Howrah
desc: The Great Banyan of the Calcutta garden — a single tree become a forest, dropping aerial roots until it covers a quarter-hectare grove — the banyan as immortal tree-of-life made fact.
credit: Ficus benghalensis, Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose garden; photo CC

name: Mughal Tree of Life Carpet
desc: A Mughal carpet flowering with the Tree of Life — flowering plants naturalized with botanist's eyes, the Persian tree re-planted in the gardens of the Great Mughals.
credit: Woven carpet, Mughal; photo public domain / CC

name: Mahabodhi Temple
desc: The Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya, raised beside the very seat of the Buddha's awakening — the descendants of the original Bodhi tree still shading pilgrims after 2,300 years.
credit: Brick temple, Bodh Gaya; photo public domain / CC

name: Bodhi Tree Worship (Sanchi)
desc: The aniconic Buddha as the Bodhi tree itself on Sanchi's gateways — worshippers kneeling before an empty throne beneath the leaves, the tree as the Enlightened One.
credit: Stone torana relief, Sanchi; photo public domain / CC

name: Bodhi Tree of Bharhut
desc: The Bharhut railing carved with the Bodhi tree of Bodh Gaya, worshipped by kings and nagas — the earliest surviving sculpture of the tree of awakening.
credit: Stone relief, Indian Museum Kolkata; photo public domain / CC

name: Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi
desc: The Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi of Anuradhapura — a sapling of the Buddha's own tree, carried by the nun Sanghamitta — the oldest documented living human-planted tree on Earth.
credit: Ficus religiosa, Anuradhapura; photo CC

name: Borobudur
desc: Borobudur — the great Javanese stupa as a carved stone mountain, its galleries circling toward emptiness like a walker circling the world-tree to its crown.
credit: Borobudur temple; photo public domain / CC

name: The Trees of Ta Prohm
desc: The strangler figs and silk-cotton trees of Ta Prohm, swallowing the Khmer monastery root by root — the jungle's own tree of life repossessing the temple of the Buddha.
credit: Tetrameles nudiflora, Angkor; photo public domain / CC

name: Xiwangmu, Queen Mother of the West
desc: Xiwangmu in her western paradise beneath the peach tree of immortality, guarded by the moon-hare and the nine-tailed fox — the Taoist goddess of the immortal orchard.
credit: Chinese painting; photo public domain / CC

name: Jōmon Sugi
desc: Jōmon Sugi, the primeval cedar of Yakushima's moss-forest — a tree old beyond record, sacred to Shintō since before Japan had a name.
credit: Cryptomeria japonica, Yakushima; photo CC

name: Shinboku — the Rope-Bound Tree
desc: A shinboku, the sacred tree of a Shintō shrine, bound with the rice-straw rope of the kami — the living tree itself as the body of the god.
credit: Sacred tree with shimenawa; photo CC

name: The Garden of the Hesperides
desc: The Hesperides among their golden apples on the tree Ladon guards at the world's western edge — the Greek tree of immortal life, Herakles' eleventh labor.
credit: Greek vase painting; photo public domain / CC

name: The Sacred Olive of Athena
desc: The Erechtheion, sheltering the mark of Poseidon's trident and Athena's sacred olive — the goddess' gift of the tree that made Athens, replanted after the Persians burned it and sprouting again.
credit: Temple, Acropolis; photo public domain / CC

name: The Sacred Oak of Dodona
desc: The oak of Zeus at Dodona, where the god spoke in the rustling leaves and priestesses read the wind — Greece's oldest oracle, a tree that answered.
credit: Sanctuary of Dodona; photo public domain / CC

name: Pakal's Sarcophagus Lid
desc: Pakal the Great falling down the World Tree to Xibalba and rising as the maize god — the Maya axis mundi carved in one vast limestone lid.
credit: Sarcophagus lid, Palenque; photo public domain / CC

name: Izapa Stela 5
desc: Izapa Stela 5, the richest of Izapan carvings — a great branching tree with figures on both sides of its waters — called by some the oldest American Tree of Life.
credit: Izapan stone; photo public domain / CC

name: World Trees of the Codex Borgia
desc: The folded pages of the Codex Borgia, where four world-trees hold the four directions and the Tlaloques pour the rains — the Mexica cosmos as a grove of colored trees.
credit: Pre-Columbian manuscript; photo public domain / CC

name: Templo Mayor
desc: The twin temple of Tenochtitlan — war and rain, the eagle's cactus and the serpent — planted at the center of the Aztec world like a tree between earth and sky.
credit: Aztec temple, Mexico City; photo public domain / CC

name: The Sun Stone — Axis of the Fifth Sun
location: Tenochtitlan (now National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City)
desc: The Aztec Sun Stone — the fifth sun born at Teotihuacan, its rays ending in solar symbols, the face of the axis around which the Mexica world turned.
credit: Basalt disk, Mexico City; photo public domain / CC

name: Ayahuasca — the Vine of Souls
desc: Banisteriopsis caapi, the great vine of the Amazon — the 'rope of the dead' that climbs the forest canopy and carries the shaman up the world-tree of vision.
credit: Malpighiaceae vine; photo CC

name: Avenue of the Baobabs
desc: The Avenue of the Baobabs — Adansonia grandidieri giants lining a dirt road in Menabe, the upside-down tree of African myth with its roots in the sky.
credit: Adansonia grandidieri, Madagascar; photo CC

name: The Iroko
desc: The iroko, the great tree of West African religion — home of spirits, altar of Ogun and the ancestors, never cut without sacrifice — the African world-tree standing between the living and the dead.
credit: Milicia excelsa; photo CC

name: The Boab
desc: The boab of the Kimberley, the hollow-bellied prison tree of Dreaming stories — Adansonia gregorii, the ancestral tree of Australia's northwest.
credit: Adansonia gregorii; photo CC

name: Crann Bethadh — the Celtic Tree
desc: Crann Bethadh, the Tree of Life of the Celts — the oak of the druids connecting sky, sea and land, its memory coiled into high crosses and knotwork branches.
credit: Celtic carving; photo public domain / CC

name: Tree of Life (Stoclet Frieze)
desc: Gustav Klimt's Tree of Life in the Stoclet dining room — the expectant embrace, the golden spiral branches, the only landscape the master ever painted.
credit: Gustav Klimt, Stoclet Frieze; photo public domain / CC

name: The Bronze Gates of Balawat
desc: The bronze bands of Shalmaneser III's gates, repoussé with the sacred tree between campaigns — the Assyrian world-tree marching with the army.
credit: Bronze repoussé, British Museum; photo public domain / CC

name: Treasures of Ur — the Great Death Pit
location: Royal Cemetery of Ur (now British Museum / Penn Museum)
desc: The gold, lapis and carnelian of Ur's royal cemetery — trees and rosettes of the Sumerian garden of the dead, dug from the soil between the rivers.
credit: Sumerian goldwork; photo public domain / CC

name: Tree-Goddess Amulet
desc: A small amulet of the sycamore goddess with her offering vessel — Hathor-Nut of the West, the tree that feeds the dead, carried on the living.
credit: Egyptian amulet; photo public domain / CC

name: Nut, the Sky-Tree Mother
desc: The sky-goddess Nut arched over the earth, her hands at the western and eastern horizons — mother of the sun who dies in her mouth and is born from her womb as the morning sycamore.
credit: Tomb painting / papyrus; photo public domain / CC

name: Hagia Sophia — the Golden Vine
desc: The golden vines and verdant marble of Justinian's Hagia Sophia — the Byzantine church as a garden, its columns grown like a forest beneath the dome of heaven.
credit: Byzantine mosaic and marble, Hagia Sophia; photo public domain / CC

name: The Transfiguration Apse (Sinai)
desc: The apse mosaic of Saint Catherine's monastery at Sinai — Christ in a mandorla of light, the bush that burned and was not consumed, rays falling like branches over the prophets.
credit: Byzantine mosaic, Sinai; photo public domain / CC

name: The Alhambra — the Walled Garden of Paradise
desc: The Alhambra's Court of the Lions, water running from the fountain through four rivers of marble — the Nasrid palace as the Quran's garden beneath which rivers flow, carved in stucco groves.
credit: Nasrid architecture, Granada; photo public domain / CC

name: Qur'anic Garden Illumination
desc: The illuminated borders of the Mamluk and Ottoman Qur'an — gold vines and palm-blossoms growing around the promise of the garden beneath which rivers flow.
credit: Manuscript illumination; photo public domain / CC
artist: Ali ibn Muhammad al-Mukattib al-Ashrafi / Ibrahim al-Amidi

name: Chahār Bāgh — the Persian Paradise Avenue
desc: The Chahār Bāgh avenue of Safavid Isfahan, a garden-city's spine of plane trees and water — the Achaemenid paradise evolved into a city's tree of life.
credit: Safavid urban garden, Isfahan; photo CC

name: The Vajrāsana — Diamond Throne
desc: The Vajrāsana, the sandstone throne Ashoka placed at the foot of the Bodhi tree — the diamond seat where the earth herself witnessed the Buddha's awakening.
credit: Mauryan sculpture, Bodh Gaya; photo public domain / CC

name: The Pine of Longevity
desc: The bungeana pines of Chinese temples — bark flaked like clouds, bent by centuries into dragons — the pine of longevity planted beside every hall of the immortals.
credit: Pinus bungeana; photo CC

name: The Ginkgo — the Living Fossil Tree
desc: The ginkgo, sole survivor of a genus 200 million years old, planted at Chinese and Japanese temples as the tree of endurance — leaves like golden fans falling at equinox.
credit: Ginkgo biloba; photo CC

name: Araucaria — the Sacred Monkey-Puzzle
desc: The araucaria groves of the Mapuche — pehuen trees of the Andean slopes, sacred to the people who take their name from them, their seeds the bread of the mountain gods.
credit: Araucaria araucana; photo CC

name: The Giant Sequoia
desc: The giant sequoias of the Sierra — the largest living things on Earth, elders of 3,000 years held sacred by the Sierra tribes, each a standing biography of the continent.
credit: Sequoiadendron giganteum; photo CC

name: The Western Red Cedar
desc: The western red cedar, the tree-of-life of the Pacific Northwest coast — the Longhouse Lifegiver from whose body the peoples cut houses, canoes, boxes and totems.
credit: Thuja plicata; photo CC

name: The Breadfruit — Tree of Navigators
desc: The breadfruit carried across the Pacific in canoes — the tree of Bounty mutiny and of island life itself, planted as a blessing for unborn generations.
credit: Artocarpus altilis; photo CC

name: The Baobab — the Upside-Down Tree
desc: The African baobab — the upside-down tree of a thousand folk tales, the tree the gods planted in anger and threw back roots-to-sky — water-hoarding giant of the savanna, home of spirits.
credit: Adansonia digitata; photo CC

name: The Stelae of Aksum
desc: The granite stelae of Aksum, carved like multi-story towers with false doors and beam-ends — stone trees raised over the kings of Ethiopia, roots of a Christian-African world-axis.
credit: Aksumite stelae; photo public domain / CC
artist: A. Davey from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest

name: Kanaga Mask of the Dogon
desc: The Dogon kanaga mask — the cruciform of Amma's creative hand and the falling nommo, danced at dama funerals to complete the tree of the world's order.
credit: Dogon wood mask; photo public domain / CC

name: Coolabah of the Watercourses
desc: The coolabah, shade-tree of the inland waterholes in Waltzing Matilda country — in Aboriginal tradition the tree of the waters, where the rainbow serpent sleeps beneath its roots.
credit: Eucalyptus coolabah; photo CC

name: The Garden Room — Villa of Livia
desc: The painted garden of Livia's villa — walls dissolved into a birdsong paradise of laurels, pomegranates and cypresses, an eternal spring grown indoors for an empress.
credit: Roman fresco, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme; photo public domain / CC

name: The Investiture of Zimri-Lim
location: Royal Palace of Mari, Syria (now Louvre)
desc: The wall-painting of King Zimri-Lim and Ishtar beneath date palms and flowing vases — the Mesopotamian sacred tree granting legitimacy to the throne of Mari.
credit: Old Babylonian mural, Louvre; photo public domain / CC

name: The Mulberry Tree (Van Gogh)
desc: Van Gogh's mulberry in the asylum garden at Saint-Rémy — a single tree burning gold against the blue, roots gripping the rock of a world the painter could not keep.
credit: Vincent van Gogh, 1889; public domain

name: The Gray Tree (Mondrian)
desc: Mondrian's early tree — branches dissolving into cubist lattice, the world-tree abstracting toward the vertical and horizontal, a theosophist's Tree of Life losing its leaves to geometry.
credit: Piet Mondrian; public domain

name: Red and White Plum Trees (Kōrin)
desc: Ogata Kōrin's paired plum trees — one austere white, one blooming crimson — across a golden river: the Rinpa master's flat, luminous world-tree in gold leaf and tarashikomi.
credit: Ogata Kōrin, folding screen; public domain

name: Old Trees, Level Distance (Guo Xi)
desc: Guo Xi's ink scroll of ancient trees receding into mist — the literati cosmology in which gnarled pines are elders, mist is breath, and distance itself is a spiritual exercise.
credit: Guo Xi, handscroll, Metropolitan Museum of Art; public domain

name: Tree of Life Tapestry (Morris & Co.)
desc: The Arts and Crafts Tree of Life — William Morris's medievalist vine, coiling acanthus and fruiting boughs woven at Merton Abbey, sacred nature redeemed by the hand of the craftsman.
credit: Morris & Co. design; photo public domain / CC

name: Tree of Life Window (Tiffany Studios)
desc: The Tiffany Studios Tree of Life — a symmetrical vine in opalescent glass, roots and crown mirroring in leaded light, the American Gothic window become a luminous world-axis.
credit: Tiffany Studios, leaded glass; photo public domain / CC

name: Palampore — the Coromandel Tree of Life
desc: The palampore — a chintz tree of life drawn and dyed on the Coromandel Coast for the world's beds and altars: one flowering stem rooted in a mound, branching into peacocks, moths and lotus.
credit: Indian chintz, mordant-dyed cotton; photo public domain / CC

name: Árbol de la Vida — Tree of Life Candelabra
desc: The Metepec tree of life — a clay candelabra flowering with Adam and Eve, mermaids, cactus and doves, the Tree of Eden retold in Talavera color by generations of Mexican family workshops.
credit: Mexican folk pottery; photo public domain / CC

name: Pipal Tree Seal of the Indus
desc: The unicorn and pipal seals of Harappa — a leaf-veined ficus religiosa standing on a platform above worshippers, the oldest script-less testament to a sacred tree, four thousand years old.
credit: Indus Valley steatite seal; photo public domain / CC
artist: Ernest John Henry Mackay (5 July 1880 – 2 October 1943)

name: The Djed Pillar — Backbone of Osiris
desc: The djed pillar — four crossbars like a lopped trunk, the backbone of Osiris and the tree-stump of the buried god, raised at the Sed festival to steady the axis of the world.
credit: Egyptian amulet / relief; photo public domain / CC

name: The Ardre Image Stone
desc: The carved slabs of Gotland — Odin, Thor fishing the serpent, and a rider beneath the arch of the world-tree: Viking cosmology chiseled into limestone flagstones that raised the dead.
credit: Viking picture stone, Gotland; photo public domain / CC

name: The Cedars of God — Horsh Arz el-Rab
desc: The Cedars of God — the last ancient grove of the Lebanon cedar, timber of Solomon's temple and Gilgamesh's forbidden forest, a thousand survivors standing in their own sanctuary.
credit: Cedrus libani; photo public domain / CC

name: The Olives of Gethsemane
desc: The eight gnarled olives of Gethsemane — scientifically dated to the era of Christ, their roots older than their trunks, witnesses at the foot of the Mount of Olives.
credit: Olea europaea, Jerusalem; photo public domain / CC

name: The Olive Tree of Vouves
desc: The Monumental Olive of Vouves — a Minoan-era tree still bearing fruit, its hollow trunk a cathedral of grain, the great mother of the Mediterranean's oil-giving tree of life.
credit: Olea europaea, Crete; photo public domain / CC

name: Shalimar Bagh — the Mughal Paradise
desc: Jahangir's Shalimar Bagh — terraces of chinar and water falling through marble pavilions along Dal Lake, the Persian chahār bāgh rebuilt in Kashmir as a Quranic garden for an empress.
credit: Mughal garden, Srinagar; photo public domain / CC

name: The Totem Pole — Cedar Column
desc: The totem pole — a western red cedar carved with raven, bear and thunderbird rising crest above crest, the coast peoples' genealogy raised as a living column between earth and sky.
credit: Pacific Northwest carved cedar; photo public domain / CC
artist: B.C. Printing & Litho Ltd.Jasper National Park (Alta.): Publisher

name: Akshaya Vata Tree of Life (Pattachitra)
desc: Pattachitra scroll painting of the Akshaya Vata, the imperishable banyan of Hindu myth regarded as a Tree of Life that survives the dissolution of the world.
credit: Own work

name: Madhubani Tree of Life
desc: Hand-painted Madhubani folk art from Bihar with a central tree framed by birds and figures; the tree is a recurring motif of life, fertility and cosmic connection in Mithila painting.
credit: Own work

name: Squirrels in a Plane Tree (Mughal miniature)
location: British Library, India Office Collections, London
desc: Mughal miniature by Abu'l Hasan and Ustad Mansur showing squirrels in a flowering plane tree, a celebrated study of a living tree from the Jahangir-era atelier.
credit: Self-scanned

name: Krishna Fluting Under a Tree
desc: Indian miniature of Krishna playing the flute beneath a blossoming tree, from the Edwin Binney 3rd Collection; the flowering tree frames the divine musician as a symbol of living nature.
credit: Flickr

name: Buddha Under the Bodhi Tree (10th Karmapa thangka)
location: Rubin Museum of Art, New York (Karmapa 900 project)
desc: Thangka by Chöying Dorje, the Tenth Karmapa, depicting Siddhartha beneath the Bodhi Tree on the verge of enlightenment, surrounded by Mara's legions.
credit: http://www.karmapa900.org/contributions_10th.html
artist: Chöying Dorje, 10th Karmapa, Photo by Karl Debreczeny

name: Bodhi Tree Thangka, Weherahena Temple
desc: Thangka-style painting of the Buddha under the Bodhi Tree at Weherahena Temple in southern Sri Lanka, continuing the iconography of the tree of awakening.
credit: Self-photographed ,  http://mstyslav-chernov.com/

name: Kalamkari Tree of Life Textile
desc: Kalamkari ('pen-work') hand-painted or block-printed cotton textile from Andhra Pradesh, whose temple-cloth tradition features the flowering tree of life amid vegetal scrollwork.
credit: Own work

name: Describing the Doctrine Under a Tree (Dunhuang silk banner)
desc: Silk banner painting from the Dunhuang caves showing a teacher expounding the doctrine beneath a tree; discovered at Mogao and now in the British Museum.
credit: 15:04, 4 April 2010 image only: Zhongguo gu dai shu hua jian ding zu (中国古代书画鑑定组). 1997. Zhongguo hui hua quan ji (中国绘画全集). Zhongguo mei shu fen lei qu

name: Naesosa Dangsan Sacred Tree
location: Naesosa Temple, Buan County, North Jeolla, South Korea
desc: The thousand-year-old dangsan namu (sacred village-tree) at Naesosa Temple, honored with ritual offerings as guardian tree linking the human and spirit worlds.
credit: Own work

name: Suhan Village Dangsan Tree
location: Suhan Village, Gurye County, South Korea
desc: Dangsan namu, the sacred tree of Suhan Village in Gurye, the focus of the dangsan-je village ritual that honors the tree as dwelling of protective spirits.
credit: Own work

name: Tamagushi (Sakaki Offering Branch)
desc: A Shinto priest presenting a tamagushi — an offering branch of the sacred sakaki tree (Cleyera japonica) decked with paper shide streamers, the evergreen that invites kami to descend.
credit: Own work

name: Sakaki Votive Offering, Katori Jingū
desc: Votive offering ensemble at Katori Jingū including a potted sakaki tree with sake, rice and vegetables — the sacred evergreen at the heart of Shinto worship.
credit: Own work

name: Shinbashira (Pagoda Heart-Pillar)
desc: Diagram of the shinbashira, the freestanding central pillar of a Japanese five-story pagoda; tradition holds it derives from the sacred tree-trunk axis that anchors the tower between heaven and earth.
credit: Own work

name: The Oath of Omladina under the Slavic Linden Tree (Mucha)
desc: Alphonse Mucha's poster 'The Oath of Omladina under the Slavic Linden Tree' — the linden (lípa) as national world-tree under which young Slavs swear brotherhood.
credit: Own work

name: Kongo Cosmogram (Dikenga)
desc: The dikenga dia Kongo or 'Yowa' cross — the Bakongo cosmogram whose rotating sun-cross maps birth, life, death and rebirth around the great axis linking the world of the living with the world of the dead.
credit: Own work

name: Kongo Cosmogram, First African Baptist Church
location: First African Baptist Church, Savannah, Georgia, USA
desc: Kongo cosmograms engraved into the floorboards of the First African Baptist Church in Savannah by enslaved Bakongo worshippers — the sacred cross carried across the Atlantic.
credit: Own work

name: Dogon Divination Table
desc: Dogon divination table, whose fox-tracking cosmology descends from the Dogon creation myth in which the world's order is revealed through signs traced in earth.
credit: Own work

name: St George Mural, Narga Selassie, Lake Tana
location: Church of Narga Selassie, Dek Island, Lake Tana, Ethiopia
desc: Wall painting of St George in the round church of Narga Selassie on Lake Tana; Ethiopian church murals frame holy scenes in lush vegetal borders echoing the paradisal tree.
credit:
St. George Slaying The Dragon 
 
  Uploaded by  Elitre
artist: A. Davey  from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest

name: St George Mural, Lalibela Rock Church
desc: Thirteenth-century rock-cut church painting at Lalibela illuminated by a shaft of sun — part of the mural programme of Ethiopia's monolithic churches.
credit:
St. George and the Dragon, Lalibela, Ethiopia 
 
  Uploaded by  Elitre
artist: A. Davey  from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest

name: Iroko Wood Carving
desc: Carved artwork made from iroko (Milicia excelsa), the tree revered in Yoruba and Igbo belief as the dwelling of powerful spirits and a bridge between earth and sky.
credit: Own work

name: Chichilaki (Georgian New Year Tree)
desc: The chichilaki, a Georgian New Year tree made of shaved hazelnut or walnut wood curled into a white beard-like canopy, said to represent the beard of St Basil or the tree of life.
credit: Own work

name: Sogdian Mural, Panjakent
desc: Wall painting from Panjakent, the eastern capital of Sogdia, whose banquet and garden scenes preserve the Iranian sacred-tree and paradise-garden imagery of pre-Islamic Central Asia.
credit: https://www.pinterest.it/pin/300826450093790824/

name: Panjakent Banquet Mural (detail)
location: Panjakent, Tajikistan (National Museum of Antiquities, Dushanbe)
desc: Detail of a banquet scene from the Panjakent murals; Sogdian elite halls paired feasting imagery with vegetal and tree motifs drawn from Iranian paradise symbolism.
credit: https://twitter.com/ccsahner/status/1133695337066110976?lang=fr

name: Simurgh-robed Delegate, Afrasiab Murals
desc: Detail from the Afrasiab 'Ambassadors' Painting' showing a delegate whose robe bears the simurgh — the mythical bird that perches on the tree of all seeds in Iranian cosmology.
credit: This image has been  extracted  from another file
artist: Painting: Unknown 7th century artist. Photographer: undetermined

name: The Felling of the Great Oak (Kalevala)
desc: Joseph Alanen's painting of the Kalevala's cosmic oak: a giant fells the monstrous oak that darkened the world, while tiny Väinämöinen marvels — the Finnish world-tree whose acorn shaded all the land.
credit: https://www.facebook.com/tampereentaidemuseo/photos/a.130671833629489/3450606881635951/

name: Khachkars of Dadivank Monastery
desc: Thirteenth-century Armenian khachkars at Dadivank Monastery; the cross-stone's wings sprout branches, palmettes and pomegranate vines so the cross becomes a flowering tree of life.
credit: Own work

name: Gunungan / Kayon (Wayang Life-Tree Puppet)
desc: Wayang kulit gunungan or kayon ('life-tree') puppet of buffalo hide — the mountain-tree emblem planted at the start and end of every Javanese shadow-play, symbolizing the cosmic tree and the whole world.
credit: Wereldmuseum Amsterdam

name: Gunungan Kayon, Wayang Kulit Banjar
desc: Plate from an album of Banjar shadow puppets showing the gunungan/kayon, the tree-mountain figure that opens and closes a wayang performance as a symbol of the cosmos.
credit: http://repositori.kemdikbud.go.id/8166/

name: Coptic Textile: Dancers Among Plants
desc: Coptic wall-hanging fragment with dancers amid vines and plants — late-antique Egyptian weavers filled textiles with the flowering tree and vine-scroll motifs of paradise.
credit: Own work

name: Roman Coin: Judaea Capta Palm Tree
location: Portable Antiquities Scheme find, United Kingdom
desc: Copper-alloy dupondius or as of Titus with the IUDAEA CAPTA reverse: a captive seated beneath a date palm — the Judean palm tree rendered as emblem of a conquered land on Roman coinage.
credit: https://finds.org.uk/database/ajax/download/id/218592  Catalog:  https://finds.org.uk/database/images/image/id/218592/recordtype/artefacts  Artefact:

name: Tlingit Totem Pole, Tongass Village Island
desc: Tlingit totem pole from Tongass Village Island topped by a brown bear; Tlingit poles are crest-tree monuments in which clan ancestry rises through the figures like the branches of a lineage tree.
credit: Own work

name: K'alyaan Totem Pole (Kiks.ádi Clan)
desc: The K'alyaan totem pole of the Tlingit Kiks.ádi Clan, erected to commemorate those lost in the 1804 Battle of Sitka; the carved cedar trunk carries the clan's raven-crest narrative upward.
credit: Transferred from   en.wikipedia   to Commons by  SchuminWeb  using  CommonsHelper .
artist: The original uploader was  Lordkinbote  at  English Wikipedia .

name: Kukui Tree (Hawaiian Enlightenment Tree)
desc: The kukui (Aleurites moluccanus), Hawaii's state tree: its oily nuts gave light, its wood made canoes, and it is revered as a kinolau body-form of Kamapua'a and an emblem of enlightenment and peace.
credit: Own work

name: Kukui Trees of Iao Valley
desc: Photographic plate of kukui trees in Iao Valley from Hawaiian legend literature; the valley groves of kukui were sacred and associated with the demi-god Kamapua'a.
credit: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Legends_of_gods_and_ghosts_(Hawaiian_mythology).djvu/73

name: Codex Mendoza: Quauhnahuac 'Beside the Trees'
desc: Folio of the Codex Mendoza recording tribute from the province of Quauhnahuac ('Beside the Trees'), whose place-sign is a stylized tree with fruit — Nahuatl pictography naming towns by their trees.
credit: The Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford

name: Tello Obelisk (Chavín Axis Mundi)
desc: The Tello Obelisk of Chavín de Huántar: a carved granite shaft covered with caimans, pumas, harpy eagles, snakes and plants — read as an axis mundi uniting the cosmic levels with edible and sacred species.
credit: Own work

name: Serge (Yakut Ritual World-Tree Post)
location: Tabaginsky Cape, bank of the Lena River, Sakha Republic, Russia
desc: A serge — the Sakha ritual hitching-post carved from larch — standing on the Lena riverbank; in Yakut shamanism the serge marks the world-tree to which spirit-horses are tethered between the worlds.
credit: Own work

name: Mongolian Ovoo (Shamanic Cairn-Tree)
desc: A Mongolian ovoo cairn hung with blue khadag scarves and a central tree-pole; the ovoo marks the axis where mountain and sky spirits are propitiated in Mongol shamanic culture.
credit: Own work

name: Naxi Dongba Ovoo, Lijiang
desc: A Naxi Dongba 'MaNi hillock' ovoo near Lijiang, combining Naxi cult practices with the cairn-and-tree axis; Dongba cosmology centers on a sacred tree at the world's navel.
credit: Own work

name: Tree of Life Mosaic, Hisham's Palace, Jericho
desc: The famous 'Tree of Life' mosaic in the audience hall of Hisham's Palace: two gazelles graze beneath a jeweled tree while a lion attacks the other — paradise and mortality set in tesserae.
credit: Own work

name: Arbre de l'Oubli (Tree of Forgetting), Ouidah
desc: The bronze 'Tree of Forgetting' monument on the Slave Route at Ouidah, around which captives were made to circle so they would forget their homeland — a dark tree of memory and passage.
credit: Own work

name: Iznik Prunus Blossom Tile (Saz Style)
desc: Iznik ceramic tile with a flowering prunus branch — the Ottoman saz repertoire that transformed the Chinese tree-of-life motif into blossoming sap-vine ornament across mosques and palaces.
credit: Own work

id: Tree of Jesse in Armenian miniature.jpg
name: Tree of Jesse — Armenian Icon
desc: The Tree of Jesse rendered in a miniature icon: the line of David rises from the root of Jesse, its branches blooming with the ancestors of Christ and crowned by the Virgin — a genealogical tree made sacred, drawn in the Armenian manuscript and iconographic tradition.
credit: Public domain (anonymous, Armenian)

id: Icon with the Virgin of the Tree of Jesse. 1666 (8384481474).jpg
name: Tree of Jesse with the Virgin (1666)
desc: An icon of the Tree of Jesse dating to 1666, with the Virgin enthroned at the crown of the tree and the patriarchs of the House of David ascending the branches — the Russian reading of the Old-Testament tree that bears the New.
credit: Public domain; painter of record 1666 (attributed to the circle of Theodore Poulakis)

name: Tree of Jesse (Icon of the Theotokos)
desc: A Byzantine-style icon of the Tree of Jesse by the iconographer Victor of Crete: the genealogical line of David unfurls in concentric rings around the Theotokos, the Virgin as the flowering centre of the sacred tree.
credit: Public domain; Victor of Crete (iconographer)

id: Christ the True Vine icon (Athens, 16th century).jpg
name: Christ the True Vine (Icon)
desc: An icon of Christ as the True Vine — the Johannine image of the plant whose branches are the disciples — painted in the 16th century (attributed to the circle of Leos Moskos), a New-Testament counterpart to the Old-Testament Tree of Jesse.
credit: Public domain; anonymous, possibly Leos Moskos (16th c.)

name: Tree of Jesse (Icon, 17th c.)
desc: A 17th-century icon of the Tree of Jesse: the tree of David drawn in the full iconographic canon, its canopy of ancestors shading the Christ-child, an emblem of salvation history hung in the Orthodox church.
credit: Public domain (anonymous, 17th c.)

id: Saint Anna and scenes from the Life of the Virgin.jpg
name: St. Anne and the Tree of Jesse (Icon)
desc: An icon of St. Anne (Mary's mother, Anna Porta Coeli) among scenes from the Life of the Virgin — the root and base of the Tree of Jesse, from whom the holy line of David descends to bear Christ.
credit: Public domain (anonymous icon painter)

name: Popol Vuh (Ximénez Manuscript)
era: 18th c. (1701), recording an older oral epic
desc: A page from the Popol Vuh — the K'iche' Maya creation epic in which the gods shape the world and plant the great tree at its centre. The Ximénez manuscript is the principal witness to the 'Book of the Counsel,' the Mesoamerican book of origins.
credit: Public domain; Francisco Ximénez (transcriber)

name: Popol Vuh — 'The Histories Begin'
desc: The opening of the Popol Vuh ('Empiezan las historias' — the histories begin), the creation account in which the world is made and the world-tree planted. Preserved in the Ximénez manuscript, the foundational sacred text of the K'iche' Maya.
credit: Public domain; Francisco Ximénez (transcriber)

name: Dresden Codex (Maya Sacred Book)
desc: The Dresden Codex — one of the four surviving Maya books — a painted bark-paper manuscript of ritual almanacs and cosmology, among the few pre-Columbian sacred texts to survive the burning of the Maya libraries.
credit: Public domain (pre-Columbian Maya)

name: Tree of Jesse Window (Rottingdean)
desc: A medieval stained-glass Tree of Jesse: the line of David rising in coloured light through the church window, the ancestors set as medallions along the trunk and the Virgin crowning the branches — the genealogical tree made luminous.
credit: CC BY 4.0 (photo: Antiquary)

id: Prophet King from a Tree of Jesse, stained glass, Germany 1260-70 (5459151218).jpg
name: Prophet-King, Tree of Jesse (Stained Glass)
desc: A prophet-king from a German Tree of Jesse window, c. 1260–1270: one of the crowned ancestors of David set within the sacred tree, part of a great High-Medieval glass genealogy of the House of David leading to Christ.
credit: CC BY 2.0 (photo: Sharon Mollerus)

name: Tree of Life Tableau (Nayarit Shaft Tomb)
desc: A ceramic tree-of-life tableau from a Nayarit shaft tomb: the cosmic tree with its root in the underworld, its branches carrying birds, figures and offerings — a Mesoamerican world-tree in three-dimensional clay.
credit: CC BY-SA 3.0 (photo: Madman2001)

name: Cylinder Seal Impression (Sacred-Tree Tradition)
desc: A rolled impression of a Mesopotamian cylinder seal. Cylinder seals are among the principal carriers of the sacred-tree motif in the ancient Near East — a world-tree of the gods depicted in miniature on the rolled clay.
credit: Public domain (ancient Mesopotamian)

name: The Tree of Life (Medieval)
desc: A medieval painted Tree of Life — the tree of Eden and the tree of the genealogy of David drawn as one: leaves, fruit and nested figures in a single sacred plant, the medieval emblem of creation and redemption.
credit: Public domain (anonymous medieval; photo: Paolo Riccio)
